author: henry
old: First letter in the collection. Documents the 34th NY's journey from Albany to Washington in the opening weeks of the war, including passage through Baltimore — a city where a riot had killed soldiers just weeks earlier (April 19, 1861).
final: Henry's first letter home: the 34th New York reaches Washington Friday evening after a river boat from Albany and a half-mile march through Baltimore, where twenty of his company carried loaded guns "in case of attack" but the city "rather cheered" them. In the depot he counts holes in the roof from an earlier row, and sees a volunteer accidentally killed by a dropped, loaded gun. Already mindful of his widowed mother, he declines a costly furlough, trusting she will need the eight dollars he sent more than he needs the visit.

author: henry
old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.
final: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a Union soldier's real-time account of First Bull Run reaching the capital by sound alone. He doesn't yet know whether his regiment will march or hold as city guard, and steadies himself in faith hours after a six o'clock chapel service: wherever he goes, he is ready.

author: henry
old: The "Later" postscript is written as news of the Union defeat at First Bull Run reaches Washington. Henry's regiment is ordered to move — the capital is in panic. The shift from mundane daily life ("I want to get a shirt washed") to "There has been a hard battle today" in a single letter is one of the most dramatic moments in the collection.
final: Writing from Washington, Henry fills most of this letter to his sister Frances with the ordinary rhythm of camp — five hours of daily drill, the Colonel's praise drawing three cheers, two papers to pass the dull hours, a dollar begged to wash a shirt. Then a postscript breaks the calm: "We are ordered off... There has been a hard battle today." He knows only to leave by morning, and tells her not to send the money after all.

author: james
old: First letter from James in the collection. Documents his time at West Point.

author: henry
old: Camp life update with details on guard duty along the Potomac and accidental death in regiment.
final: Writing from the Washington defenses, Henry reports his regiment posted as Potomac guards against rebel crossings — and the camp talk that it may never see a battle, to which he answers, "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where." Three days too sick to drill in fever-and-ague country, he still sends his five-dollar gold piece home by the Captain, ordering his sister and mother to spend it: "I put that down as a command." That same Sabbath a Co. H private — the regiment's third such loss — was killed when soldiers playing with their guns let one go off.

author: henry
old: References Battle of Hatteras Inlet (Aug 28-29, 1861), Henry's advice against Alexander enlisting, cannon fire into Virginia, and rumor of wintering in Kentucky. Important for Alexander's enlistment timeline.
final: From the Washington defenses, just off picket duty with Corporal Kellogg, Henry counsels his mother that Alexander "had better stay at home" — college or home over war — rather than join "Ransoms Company." Word has just reached camp of the fall of Fort Hatteras, "a noble achievement," and he wagers the war can't last two years. His regiment's two brass cannon lobbed shells three miles into Virginia last Sabbath, though the enemy "would not return the favor."

author: alexander
old: Alexander's first letter in the collection — documents his arrival at military barracks in Ogdensburgh. Vivid arrival scene with sensory detail.

author: henry
old: Brief update with interesting detail of Confederate signal flare observed from picket duty.
final: On picket duty near Washington, Henry watches a Confederate signal rise over Virginia — "somewhat like the evening star, only it was a dark red — looked very fine." Between such glimpses of the enemy he relays the small comforts of camp: a merry supper with Lieutenant Scott, word that a friend from Chazy Village addressed his last letter, and a note for Mother that he already has more clothing than he can carry.

author: henry
old: Confirms Alexander has officially enlisted ("in for the war"). False alarm incident at camp. Money being sent home via Reich.
final: Henry takes in word that his brother Alexander is "in for the war," answering with measured resignation — "Perhaps it is all for the best" — and the quiet conviction it "can't last a great while." From camp near Washington, where bombs are lobbed into Virginia and jittery guards have just fired on a white horse in a false alarm, he wraps twenty-five dollars to send home and prepares to head out two days on picket in the first cold snap of fall.

author: alexander
old: Detailed daily schedule at Camp Wheeler. Company sworn into state service on Saturday (Sept 21). Regiment over 700 men. Election of officers — Capt. Ransom and Lt. Loring E. White.

author: alexander
old: Vivid guard duty narrative — watch word compromised, guards doubled, Colonel's response. Rich detail on camp security procedures. Daily prayer meetings documented.

author: henry
old: Detailed camp life: tent improvements, guard duty, rations, card-playing ban. Corrects exaggerated report of a skirmish.
final: Writing to brother Charles, Henry corrects an inflated report of an attack across the river — not three companies of Rebels but thirty-five men against twelve — quipping, "I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand." A bad bout of rheumatism from sleeping on bare ground eased only after he and two tentmates splurged 95 cents on a tent floor, and he admits he held off writing of the illness because he couldn't spell the word. He notes the colonel's new ban on card-playing after too much gambling.

author: alexander
old: Documents the "Brother Craftsmen" mutual aid society — soldier fraternal organization with headquarters at Watertown, NY. Detailed description of camp prayer meeting. Reveals Alexander's moral framework and social isolation.

author: alexander
old: Brief logistics letter — uniforms arriving, furlough promised, travel pass needed.

author: alexander
old: Camp description, regiment numbers, company strength. Mentions possible corporal's berth for Alexander.

author: henry
old: Entire company under arrest over rope-cutting incident. Lt. Scott conflict. Military punishment details. Charles considering enlistment — Henry says join his company if he does. Chaplain sick.
final: A disciplinary crisis grips Henry's company near Washington: a soldier who left his picket early and grew abusive to Lt. Scott had his pay docked, a 30-lb knapsack strapped on, and his hands tied above his head — until a comrade cut the rope, throwing the whole company under arrest with a guard ringed around their tents. From picket duty, Henry vows he keeps clear of trouble and "tries to do what is right," even as card-playing now brings court martial and his brother Charles grows anxious to enlist.

author: henry
old: Brigadier General Gormon's inspection; regiment called "sharp shooters" in press. POW escape narrative — Kellogg confirmed prisoner in Richmond. Murder by stabbing in camp. Poolesville winter quarters rumor. James confirmed in school.
final: Henry relays a daring escape from rebel captivity: a prisoner taken in the same skirmish as Kellogg feigned illness to hoard his daily opium ration, then drugged his guard's coffee and slipped through three enemy regiments to reach camp — bringing word that Kellogg is held unwounded at Richmond. Henry also reports a man stabbed by a drunk at midnight, dead by morning, and Brig. Gen. Gormon's inspection of the regiment, lately dubbed "the sharp shooters" in the papers.

author: henry
old: Receipt of handmade portfolio from Frances. Mentions Brink (family connection). Nellie correspondence.
final: Writing from the camps around Washington, Henry thanks his sister Frances for a handmade portfolio of writing supplies — so finely made he refused to believe it wasn't store-bought ("I thought it came form the store"), and now the envy of the other boys in camp, none of whose match it. Beneath the gratitude runs a quieter homesickness: he longs for her picture and a chance to sing when she has company, and a postscript records a letter from Nellie, with a promised photograph of her own.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's regiment confirmed: 60th NY Infantry ("Sixtieth Regt. Detailed journey narrative: Camp Wheeler → Rouses Point → Whitehall → Albany → Hudson River → New York City (flag & horse presentation, Enfield rifles iss...

author: henry
old: Henry now at Camp McClellan — regiment has moved from Washington defenses. Battle formation false alarm (rebels crossing river).
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in a cold November rain, Henry tells brother Charles his regiment may see a battle before winter — and recounts the night the whole brigade formed in line of battle and marched toward the river on a false report that the rebels were crossing. Between the soldiering he sends $20 home by express, registers quiet shock at Albert Savage's death, and asks that Mother be told her preserves arrived safely.

author: henry
old: Confederate deserter crossing Potomac at night — vivid eyewitness account. Describes visible enemy (fires along river, visible in daytime). Informal cross-river trading/contact despite orders.
final: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his brother James of a drunken Confederate deserter who paddled a half-swamped boat across the Potomac to surrender to his twelve-man picket post — cursing the sentries as "sons of biches" when they demanded the countersign, then refusing to go back when the rebels called him the next morning. The enemy was visible by day and lit fires along the river by night, with orders forbidding any talk across the water. Henry kept two rebel gun caps; Lt. Scott paid five dollars for the deserter's knife.

author: henry
old: Brigade composition confirmed: Gorman is General. Brigade includes three NY regiments (including 2nd NY), Minnesota regiment, and 34th NY.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry sketches his brigade's order of battle: three New York regiments including the 2nd, the Minnesota regiment, and his own, all drilling together two or three times a week under General Gorman. He has shaken off a bout of homesickness, and gently corrects the rumors reaching home that his company has suffered — "It is not correct" — admitting only one hard stretch in Virginia, while his sister Frances spins plans for the day he comes back.

author: henry
old: Winter conditions, furlough queue, Thanksgiving on picket, picture taken, farm concerns, tax willingness.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in cold so sharp he can scarcely hold his pen, Henry begs his worrying mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease," reports he stands third or fourth in the furlough queue, and came off picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock. He confesses he sometimes thinks he "did wrong to leave home" with the farm needing him that winter, yet pledges that "when I do get home I shall stay."

author: alexander
old: Alexander's unit definitively confirmed: Co. H, 60th NY Volunteers ("Sixtieth Regt.

author: alexander
old: James had Orderly Sergeant offer (needed 5 men) — turned it down. James has chance at West Point — Alexander strongly encourages education over enlistment.

author: alexander
old: Photography details — two pictures taken in Baltimore (one with Luther, one solo). Shows photographic economy of Civil War soldiers.

author: alexander
old: Eyewitness account of freight train boiler explosion — one of the most detailed civilian/military incident narratives in the collection. Ransom's miraculous survival.

author: henry
old: Winter quarters forming — Minnesota regiments building log houses, 34th NY building hospital. Tent mates identified (E. Graves from Chazy, John Green, A. Perkins). Sutler drummed out for selling liquor. Colonel L--- resigned (considered coward). Henry hasn't connected with Alexander yet — wrong address.
final: From Camp McClellan, two days before Christmas, Henry expects his regiment to settle into winter quarters guarding the Potomac — the Minnesota regiments are raising log houses and his own is building a hospital, signs enough that "this looks somewhat like staying." Camp discipline tightens around him: the old sutler drummed out for selling liquor, gamblers made to stand on a barrel six hours without food. Tenting among strangers and still unable to reach his brother Alexander, he confesses he gets very lonesome now and then, wishing for the Champlain boys instead.

author: henry
old: B. Miner carrying letters to Champlain (private mail carrier). Accordion lessons from Bill Robers. Journal discontinued due to cold — Henry regrets this. Eight rebel deserters crossed to Union side, report rebels have nothing to eat. Capt. Rich preached. Poolesville ~3 miles from camp.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry reports eight rebels crossing the lines as deserters with word that the enemy "have nothing to eat" — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac. With little else to tell in the sameness of winter quarters, he confesses the cold has stopped his journal, a thing he'll be sorry for if he gets home, and admits he'd give much to be back for the village sing school.

author: henry
old: Brigade drill — Gen. Gorman complimented 34th NY ("did the best of them all"). Henry still can't reach Alexander — directed to Washington but that's wrong (should be Baltimore). Henry doesn't know Alexander's regiment. Moral commentary on swearing and gambling. Same gambling punishment as LTR-1861-12-19-001. Accidental self-shooting in Minnesota Regt.
final: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry writes his mother with a soldier's pride: at brigade drill Gen. Gorman told the regiment "they did the best of them all" — "we felt quite proud, I tell you." Yet he still cannot reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington on a direction now proving wrong, the regiment unknown to him: "It seems bad that we cannot correspond." Unsettled by the swearing and gambling around him — four men caught at cards face six hours on a barrel — Henry insists a man keeps good morals in camp only if "very strict and firm."

author: alexander
old: Company H moved to Baltimore proper — ordered to replace Company C at Camden Station (B&O Railroad depot). Quartered in 3-story brick building on city outskirts.

author: alexander
old: Preston King in Baltimore — U. Senator from NY, reportedly trying to have 60th NY sent north to guard frontiers (Trent Affair context).

author: henry
old: Henry finally received a letter from Alexander — direction "not quite correct" but it arrived. Alexander wrote about Capt.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from his brother Alexander — the letter found him despite a direction "not quite correct" — and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between a $3.50 sheet-iron stove bought against the cold and a promise to send $25 home next pay day, Henry sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.

author: alexander
old: Most detailed guard duty description in entire collection — sentinel orders verbatim, corporal relief procedures, 2-hour rotation, night firing protocol, camp alarm sequence.

author: alexander
old: NCO warrant received — formal appointment as Corporal, with commission language quoted verbatim ("Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence in the patriotism, valor, fidelity and abilities of Alexander F.

author: henry
old: New Year's 1862 at Camp McClellan: Beer from Captain, some boys drunk. Company presented Capt.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan after a New Year's of beer "from the Capt." and a few boys gone too drunk, Henry tells his mother his company has presented Capt. Reich a $125 sword — he gave a dollar on a private's pay, "some gave more and some less." The Minnesota band played most all night before the Colonel's tent. He longs for a furlough, but only married men may go, so he waits — lonesome for letters and the box of socks still stuck in Washington.

author: henry
old: Henry burned all home letters — knapsack space and anticipation of moving into Virginia. "Please burn all my letters" — if obeyed, this would have destroyed the home-side correspondence.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry admits he has burned every letter he received from home — they took up too much room in his knapsack, and he did not want them on him "if I should go over into Virginia." Then his postscript turns the request around: "Please burn all my letters." He closes glad, for her sake, that Frances is going to teach in Montreal this winter — a quiet, ordinary aside beside a plea that, obeyed, would have erased this entire correspondence.

author: alexander
old: H killed January 9 — Alexander helped recover the body ("screwed up" courage). Quotes Henry's letter (mailed Jan 6): "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living" — a prescient statement...

author: alexander
old: Moved to first platoon / headquarters — replacing Corporal Myers (sick). Now "at head quarters.

author: alexander
old: Porter (Edwin Porter) killed by train on railroad track — graphic eyewitness account. Alexander helped recover body.

author: alexander
old: Union Relief Association described — private/government funded, feeds soldiers passing through Baltimore; seating for 800+, sleeping room for a regiment. Alexander boarded there at Camden Station.

author: henry
old: Pay day accounting: $15 sent home; sutler bill $5. 50); owes band 50¢, cook 50¢, sword $1.
final: Paid off at Camp McClellan, Henry sends $15 home and itemizes a soldier's whole economy from $13-a-month pay — sutler, boots, a $1 sword installment, fifty cents each to the band and the cook. He turns down requests to lend money in camp: "I would rather send it home." Buoyed by the "glorious victory in Kentucky," he predicts the war will be over before July, even as the unhealthy barracks are burned for firewood, leaving the men in their tents the rest of the winter.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's near-miss with train — passenger train "hardly ten feet from me," one desperate jump to safety. Edwin Porter confirmed killed by cars (same incident as LTR-1862-01-17-001).

author: alexander
old: Colonel Hayward resigned — 60th NY now "Orphan Regiment. " New Colonel Green expected.

author: henry
old: Two desertions from Co. D — one from drunken scrape/guard house, one while cutting wood (when Captain was in Champlain).
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in a thaw he hopes has "broke" the heart of winter, Henry tallies two desertions from his company: one man drank himself into the guard house and bolted, another vanished while out cutting wood with the Captain away in Champlain. Amid gambling and watch lotteries he won't touch, the young soldier guards his pay and his pledge not to drink, and sits twice for photographs beside his tent-mate Graves.

author: henry
old: 34th NY and Gorman's Brigade marched to Harpers Ferry. Departed Camp McClellan → 20-mile march → camped overnight (cold, no shelter) → Adams Town → 30-mile freight train ride → Harpers Ferry.
final: Writing from Camp Gorman two miles from Harpers Ferry, Henry recounts his regiment's hard march to the front: twenty miles the first day, then a freezing night under nothing but blankets and sky, up at three for coffee and a hard cracker. He finds the town "a perfect wreck" — buildings burnt to their walls, the bridge gone, a locomotive lying in the river. Crossing the Potomac on a bridge of boats, the 34th was called the best-looking regiment to pass over.

author: henry
old: Detailed march narrative — parallel account to LTR-1862-02-05-001 with additional details: passed through Barnesville; "very short notice" to march; Col.
final: Writing to his brother Charles from Camp Bolivar Heights, Henry recounts the 34th's sudden march on "very short notice" — out at three in the morning on coffee, hard crackers, and salt junk, through Barnesville to Adamstown, then thirty miles by freight car into Harpers Ferry, with Col. Ladue back at the regiment's head. Billeted in a cotton factory, the men ground its stored wheat through the floors until Gen. Gorman laughed he "did not know what to do with them." Crammed now seventeen to a bell tent, Henry confesses he'd rather be home to make sugar this spring, "but that is out of the question."

author: henry
old: Routine morale letter from winter quarters. Documents camp conditions, religious provisions (Testament and Psalms), and clarifies a false rumor about Lt. Scott's loyalty. Provides timeline checkpoint: Henry enlisted ~June 1, sworn in June 15, in service ~9 months by this date.
final: Writing from a bell tent at Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, his letter steadied on his knee for want of a table, Henry sets his mother's mind at rest about a rumor that had reached home: Lieut. Scott was arrested not for communicating with the rebels but for falling asleep as officer of the guard. Some in the company dislike Scott; Henry says he likes him very well himself. He prizes the company's gift of a Testament and Psalms, and reckons he has now been in the service "a little over nine months."

author: alexander
old: Shows inter-regimental communication: Alexander (60th NY, Baltimore) exchanges letters with Henry (34th NY, likely at different location), indicates family network among brothers in service. Demonstrates officer kindness (Capt. Ransom) and shows regiments receiving civilian visitors/correspondence from Poolesville area. Alludes to James's academic situation and family pressure to succeed (pre-West Point confirmation).

author: alexander
old: CRITICAL SOURCE: West Point appointment for James Hubbell CONFIRMED as of Feb. This is a major turning point in the Hubbell family narrative.

author: henry
old: CRITICAL CHRONOLOGICAL ANCHOR: Henry's presence at Camp McClellan on Feb. 11 — 13, 1862, directly contradicts the Feb.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry answers Charles's question about soldiers allotting pay home with an unvarnished ledger of camp life: many in his company spend their wages at the sutler's, including George Dodds, now borrowing — though Henry asks Charles not to repeat it. He lays out the ten-day ration cycle and the indignity of eating "dog fashion" without tin plates, joking that "a pound or two of dirt" is "good enough for soldiers." A drunken row that night ended at the guard house, a Mexican War veteran schooling the officer of the day on the rules of arrest.

author: henry
old: Eyewitness reporting of major Civil War victory: Henry documents the Burnside Expedition's victory in South Carolina (Battle of Roanoke Island, Feb.
final: Henry writes his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, passing the night's electric news: "the glorious victory in South Carolina" by the Burnside Expedition, two thousand prisoners taken, met with "great cheering" through the camp. Eager and untested, he boasts that once the 34th goes into action "the rebels will have to run" — then notes, plainly, that the farms down here are "all worked by slaves."

author: henry
old: Brief morale letter from Camp McClellan. Provides snapshot of soldier experience: guard duty as most difficult aspect, drunkenness and fighting in company, mild weather, homesickness. Reports receiving multiple letters from Alexander (evidence of inter-regimental correspondence). Shows mother's letters as significant morale booster.
final: From Camp McClellan in mud and unseasonably mild weather, Henry calls guard duty "the hardest of soldiering" — up nearly all night — yet admits he has grown so used to it he hardly minds, and longs to "make a move of some kind." He grieves the heavy drunkenness and fighting in his company but insists he keeps clear of it, and tells his mother that nothing does a soldier so much good as a letter from home.

author: alexander
old: MULTI-FACETED MAJOR SOURCE: (1) Alexander's college decision: He declines college at this moment, preferring to stay in service and work farm/family business. Plans to be "well fitted" before attending.

author: alexander
old: Documents soldier's sabbath observance, religious life, and church attendance in occupied Baltimore. Shows postal economics of war period and family postage hardship. Provides evidence of inter-company communication (Corporal Perkins, Henry's messmate). Reveals family correspondence delays and Aunt Laurie's negligent letter-writing. Establishes Alexander's playful tone and humor. Request for Plattsburgh (NY) newspaper indicates interest in home region news.

author: henry
old: Orders to march — knapsacks packed, ready at a moment's notice. Read at dress parade.
final: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother the order has come — read at dress parade, the men to pack their knapsacks and stand ready to march at a moment's notice, surplus clothes boxed off to Poolesville. The night before, the chaplain had preached on "the Duty of Patriotism" and doubted they would see another Sabbath in camp, heavy firing already sounding across the river. He notes Col. Ladue's return and rumored promotion to brigadier general, then closes urging his mother not to worry: he has good health now.

author: henry
old: RESOLVES DATING DISCREPANCY: "Our Regt. Left Camp McClellan on the 26th.
final: Henry writes his mother from Harpers Ferry that the regiment "Left Camp McClellan on the 26th," marching through Poolesville, Barnesville, and Adamstown, then taking the cars and crossing into the gutted town on a floating bridge of boats. He reckons some 60,000 troops are massed here and — eager for what's coming — admits he doesn't care how soon they "see some fun," the sooner the better. Yet the burnt bridge, brick walls standing over ashes, and wrecked arsenal leave him feeling "bad" at the rebels' destruction.

author: henry
old: Short addendum. Confirms Henry's regiment is in a grist mill building (previously described as cotton factory in LTR-1862-02-05-002). Rebels took wheat from this location. Too restricted to explore town (guards posted).
final: Henry writes from a large brick building that once served as a grist mill — a place, he notes wryly, where the rebels seized so much wheat "they will never have the same chance again." On a cold but pleasant March day, kept from roaming the town and from mailing his letter, he apologizes for falling short of the longer letter he'd hoped to send and promises more when he can.

author: alexander
old: Duck hunting adventure — vivid narrative of soldiers hunting in Chesapeake Bay with rifles; fog, leaking boat, broken oarlock.

author: alexander
old: James's War Department appointment confirmed — studying under Everest. Alexander wishes he could send $60.

author: alexander
old: Massive troop movements through Baltimore: 3-4,000 on Sunday alone; thousands more coming. 30 steamers for Fortress Monroe.

author: henry
old: March to Winchester and back — 34th NY and two brigades marched 30 miles from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester, found 25,000 Union troops already there. Rebels had left "probably for good.
final: Henry's regiment and two brigades marched some thirty miles on foot from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester to drive out the rebels, only to learn three miles short of the town that 25,000 Union troops already held it and the Confederates had fled "probably for good." A cavalry regiment had torn down a rebel flag at Berryville; Henry pulled picket and skirmish duty after twenty miles, owning to "a good many hardships" — yet nine months from home, he still hopes the rebellion will be over by next summer.

author: alexander
old: Refuses to burn letters — "No — no — I cannot do that. " Has kept all letters since enlistment (except some from Ogdensburg).

author: henry
old: Bell tents detailed: 16 men, bell-shaped stove in center, pole in middle, open top for smoke. Roads to Winchester: macadamized (small stone), very good in any weather.
final: Writing from Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, Henry tells his brother James the brigade expects to move soon for Washington, the Shenandoah railroad bridge repaired so the cars again run to Winchester over good macadamized roads. Sixteen men share his bell-shaped tent, a bell stove at its center, the top open for smoke; two others blew down in the night's wind. He confesses a long-neglected debt for Mrs. Douglas's flour, asks James to settle it, and adds wearily he wouldn't object if the war closed next week.

author: henry
old: 34th NY moves from Harpers Ferry to Washington — 83 miles by freight train in 24 hours. Arrived ~2 AM, marched 1+ mile to brick barracks.
final: After the railroad bridge at Harpers Ferry was finished, Henry's 34th NY rode a freight train eighty-three miles to Washington in twenty-four hours, reaching brick barracks at two in the morning to await pay before an unknown next assignment. A Sabbath in the capital, he marvels, feels nothing like one — cars running, soldiers drunk, the provost guard hauling off stragglers — and he vows to keep his pass signed and dodge arrest himself. Bread, coffee, and salt junk, he allows, still beat hard crackers.

author: alexander
old: 60th NY "struck tents" — moved from Eutaw St. quarters to Camp Preston King near Baltimore.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's 18th birthday — March 28, 1862 (writing March 30, reflecting on it). I have begun life's battle for myself.

author: alexander
old: COMPLETE DAILY SCHEDULE: 6 AM roll call → 7 breakfast → 8 guard mounting → 9 NCO drill → 10 squad drill → 11:30 inspection → 12:30 dinner → 2:30 company drill → 4:30 dress parade → 6 supper → 9 PM roll call → 9:30 taps.

author: henry
old: 34th NY moves to the Peninsula — Alexandria → steamboat → Fortress Monroe → Hampton, VA. ~200 miles in 2 days.
final: Henry writes from Hampton, Va., after the 34th New York's two-day steamboat passage from Alexandria to Fortress Monroe — nearly 200 miles down a Chesapeake Bay so wide he could see no land on either side. He finds the town burned to the ground, "worse than Harpers Ferry, every building burnt," the men penned up like sheep, sleeping under four rubber blankets buttoned into a tent. Hard crackers, no coffee — "but then we are soldiers," he shrugs, "and of course we have to put up with whatever comes in our way."

author: henry
old: Henry keeping a journal — "I have been keeping a Journal some time. " Plans to copy and send home.
final: Writing by candlelight near Fortress Monroe with roll call minutes away, Henry tells his mother he has been "keeping a Journal some time" that he means to copy and send home — even as his regiment prepares to march twenty-four miles on foot to York Town at dawn, expecting an onward movement toward Richmond. The rebels have made "a clean sweep of everything," wood is scarce, and a peddler who wandered into camp was stripped of his pies and apples in moments. Yet it is the tree toads, he confesses, that make him think of home.

author: henry
old: 25,000 troops at Hampton with one brigade. Steamer ran aground — had to transfer.
final: Writing his brother Charles from a green Hampton, Va. field shared by some twenty-five thousand troops, Henry recounts a crowded two-and-a-half-day boat passage whose steamer ran aground, forcing a transfer to reach shore. Confident after a summer of bayonet drill — "I pity the rebels" — he still admits he would rather be making sugar this spring than soldiering, and warns Charles not to let out the home sugar bush except to an honest man.

author: henry
old: Pocket diary confirmed — "I have been keeping a pocket diary, write down everything that transpires from day to day. I have 28 dates.
final: Writing from "Camp in field" as heavy musketry sounds off toward Yorktown, Henry tells his brother James he has been keeping a pocket diary — 28 dated entries recording "everything that transpires from day to day." Two days earlier his company double-quicked a mile expecting a fight, most of Co. D holding together; a captured rebel in gray overcoat looked on "very sullen." He still asks James to mind the cows and horse, hoping to be home next summer.

author: henry
old: Pioneer duty at Yorktown — detailed as pioneers with axes, picks, shovels; building roads through woods for artillery. Rebels blocked roads.
final: From a nameless "Camp in field" sixteen miles from Hampton, Henry tells his mother how his regiment spent the Sabbath detailed as pioneers — axes, picks, and shovels cutting fresh roads for the artillery through woods the retreating rebels had felled ahead of Yorktown. He records Gen. Gorman's cold counsel to keep cool in action "and not to mind if brother or cousin fell, but to go ahead," then, glimpsing McClellan twice ("a young looking man") and Virginia trees in blossom, confesses the whole campaign "is all like a dream."

author: henry
old: Rebels at York Town "pretty well surrounded. " Rebel slave reported they left on double quick.
final: Writing from camp sixteen miles from Fortress Monroe after his regiment took the boat from Alexandria, Henry reports the rebels holding York Town but "getting pretty well surrounded," and expects to march there any day for "a little skirmish." He passes along an enslaved man's account that the rebels fled "on a double quick" at word of the Union advance, dismisses them as "a cowardly set," and closes hoping to be home next June, "if the war is over."

author: alexander
old: "The little Corporal" — Alexander's nickname (smallest Corporal in company, positioned on extreme left). DeRochambeau/Yorktown comparison — second siege of Yorktown in American history.

author: henry
old: Siege of Yorktown firsthand — 3 miles from rebel lines. Called into line for expected skirmish.
final: Writing his brother Charles from camp three miles outside Yorktown, Henry relays his first secondhand battle reports — a repulsed rebel assault on a Union battery and a Vermont regiment so badly hit that one company was left with "only twenty." Carried across eight days, the letter closes with a rebel dawn attack on the 26th and a sharpshooter shot down. "Nothing livens me up more than to hear the firing cannon," Henry confesses — a green soldier still hungry for the fight he hasn't yet faced.

author: henry
old: Siege of Yorktown operations: Drums silenced and band doesn't play — fear of rebel shelling. attacked on picket — night before last, heavy musketry; rebels tried to drive pickets in but failed.
final: From the Yorktown siege lines on April 21st, 1862, Henry writes his brother James that the regiment's drums and band have gone silent "for fear that the rebels will find us out and throw shells into our camp," and recounts a driving-rain midnight alarm when the New York 2nd's pickets, attacked in force, refused to be driven in. Between five o'clock arms inspections and drills at four, he confesses he often thinks with pleasure of the spring he and James made maple sugar at home — "it is nothing to what I have been through, or may."

author: henry
old: Sedgwick's Division, Gorman Brigade — unit identification confirmed. McClellan described: "Splendid looking fellow, smiling countenance, rides a fine horse," ~200 cavalry bodyguard.
final: Writing from the siege lines near Yorktown, Henry pins down his place in the army — Sedgwick's Division, Gorman's Brigade — and watches a balloon rise each day to spy on the rebel works while McClellan, "a splendid looking fellow" with a 200-strong cavalry guard, rides past. But the war he describes is quieter than that: three hours on picket in a dark, rainy night, hearing rebels "pounding and sawing" at their works just beyond sight. Even there, his mind drifts home to the horses, the cattle, and a farm with no one to see to it.

author: alexander
old: promoted to Brig. — General Green, "desendent of old revolutionary hero General Green.

author: henry
old: Pay and financial accounting: 2 months' pay; $20 home; boots $1 (Peter Guyan); sutler $1; cook 50¢; $3. Emerson Smith used all wages.
final: Newly paid for two months at Fortress Monroe's Camp "Windfield Scott," Henry mails $20 home by express and accounts for every cent that remains — a dollar to tap his boots, fifty cents to the cook, three-fifty to spend as he pleases. Opposite a rebel fort our men raise a tower under daily shelling, and Henry rises before daylight braced for an attack he senses is coming. The Sabbath, he notes, goes unkept like any other day, though "God will not hold us accountable for what we cannot help."

author: henry
old: $20 enclosed by express. Heavy cannonading at 4 AM. Rebel fort visible from camp. On picket.
final: Writing from camp near York Town on May 1st, Henry encloses twenty dollars by express and tells his mother of a rebel fort plainly visible from his lines and heavy cannonading at four that morning. He scrawled the note between turns at picket, signing only "H.H." and closing with a son's plea to "write often."

author: henry
old: Yorktown evacuated by rebels — Henry inside fortifications. "Immense and very strong.
final: Inside the Confederate fortifications at Yorktown — abandoned overnight, "immense and very strong," sandbags built head-high — Henry writes home from within a captured rebel tent, marveling at works he calls the strongest he has seen. He recounts the hardest night of his soldiering: an all-night march in driving rain and deep mud, halting every ten paces behind stacked divisions, back to camp by two in the morning. The retreating enemy left shells buried underfoot to step on, and some of his men have already been hurt by them.

author: henry
old: West Point, VA — on York River, NOT the academy. 20-30 miles from Yorktown, ~30 from Richmond.
final: Writing his sister Frances for the first time in nearly a year, Henry reports his regiment's crowded boat passage from newly evacuated Yorktown to West Point, Virginia — a landing on the York River, he is careful to note, not the Military Academy — about thirty miles from Richmond. He marvels at the rebels' vast abandoned earthworks and dates the Yorktown bombardment to Wednesday, April 16, then promises once more to send the journal he has kept of the campaign.

author: henry
old: Cornwallis surrender spot — "pointed out to me. It was a great sight.
final: Writing from West Point on the York River, twenty-five to thirty miles from Richmond, Henry is shown the spot where Cornwallis surrendered — "a great sight," the Revolution's ground now ringed again by American troops. Word reaches him of the 16th Regiment's skirmish, one company losing sixteen, before the war narrows to a handshake with George Corbin and Royal, friends from home. Then his thoughts turn back to the farm, his mother's summer, and a newspaper stolen before he could finish it.

author: alexander
old: Railroad given up to company by 15th-20th — regiment no longer needed. wagers $25 to $1 discharged within a month.

author: henry
old: Camp Alton, West Point, VA — 34th Regt. Near unnamed river emptying into York River (likely Pamunkey or Mattaponi).
final: Writing from Camp Alton near West Point, Va., Henry reckons some hundred thousand troops are massed around him and expects the 34th to move on Richmond any day, trusting that "McClellan is working slow but sure." Word reaches him that Alexander's 60th Regt. may be bound for the same place, and he aches to see his brother even as he cautions him he'll tire of the marching soon enough. Between the lines he is just a farm boy, asking who is working the garden and where the cows are pastured.

author: alexander
old: Alexander crosses into Virginia — "for the first time planted our feet on the sacred soil of Virginia. " Harpers Ferry — 60th NY now deployed there.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's first combat experience. Slept on arms every night since arrival.

author: henry
old: George Dodds in hospital, "run down so you would not know him" — applying for discharge. Henry stood march despite being sick.
final: Marching while sick himself, Henry gently turns aside his mother's offer to come nurse him at the front — "you would be obliged to be on your feet most of the time, and I am afraid it would bring you down sick. There are others better able than you are." He reports his comrade George Dodds so wasted "you would not know him," now in the hospital and applying for a discharge, while Henry resolves to "stand it through." Apologizing for his poor pen, he encloses ten dollars and asks who is keeping his money.

author: alexander
old: 60th NY marches ~40 miles from Harpers Ferry to Winchester. (Free Footed Virginians)" — mocking Confederate retreat.

author: henry
old: Battle of Fair Oaks aftermath — regiment lost 123 wounded and killed (papers said 150). D lost 2 killed and 10 wounded.
final: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond after the Battle of Fair Oaks, Henry counts himself thankful to have come through unhurt — the regiment lost 123 killed and wounded, his own Company D two killed and ten wounded. Even Lieut. Scott, once resented by the men, won them all over by acting bravely before being wounded. Yet Henry has been three days sick on quinine, rebel shells whizzing into camp "a caution," and longs for one good meal at home: "even if it wasn't anything but potatoes and salt."

author: henry
old: BATTLE OF FAIR OAKS — FIRSTHAND COMBAT ACCOUNT. "You can have no conception of how exciting it is to be in a battle.
final: Writing from camp five miles from Richmond, Henry gives his brother Charles a firsthand account of the battle of Fair Oaks — the ground shaking, the firing "like a number of men felling trees, only much faster," loading while advancing through woods, and his own forty rounds fired before he ever knew anyone had fallen. A captured secesh tells of Richmond ladies who rode out in carriages to watch Yankees taken, then bore home their own wounded instead. Sick with dysentery, under shelling that killed a man at the hospital that morning, Henry admits he gets lonesome now and then.

author: henry
old: One year of service — "A long year it has been to me. Twelve more months.
final: Writing from camp within five miles of Richmond on the first anniversary of his regiment's muster, Henry reckons that fewer than five hundred men are now fit for duty — "a long year it has been to me." Still weak from a week under the doctor's care, he relays a captured rebel's grudging awe at how fast the Yankees could load and fire, and savors how the carriages of ladies who came to watch the Union defeat were instead pressed into carrying off the Confederate wounded.

author: alexander
old: Detailed foraging account — cherries, chickens, milk, sheep, pig. "Are you not horrified to think you have a hen roost robbing son?

author: henry
old: Henry's health in serious decline — dysentery "very bad," unable to do duty for over a week, Dr. every morning, quinine and pills.
final: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond on a Sabbath afternoon, Henry confesses to his mother that he has had the dysentery "very bad" and unable to do duty for over a week, reporting to the doctor most mornings for quinine and pills while sickness spreads through the regiment. He lists his rations in unusual detail — hard bread, salt junk, coffee, soup — and clings to McClellan's siege "starfing them out," even as he admits he is "about disgusted with soldiering" and dreams of home, where he means to sit down and eat nothing but potatoes.

author: henry
old: FAIR OAKS — BAYONET CHARGE DETAIL: "pushed right in head first. " Came to bayonet charge at woods edge.
final: Writing from camp near Richmond to his brother Charles, Henry recounts a recent bayonet charge in which his regiment, "pushed right in head first," halted at the woods' edge to fire low into kneeling rebels before they could volley — by his Colonel's account leaving three hundred dead and wounded. To Charles alone he confesses he is "almost tempted to desert sometimes," held back only by the disgrace and by his mother being all alone. He also relays how Capt. Reich, refusing an order on dress parade, was put in irons and discharged.

author: alexander
old: FALSE REPORT of Richmond's capture — "capture of Richmond has just been reported. " Dispatch to Sigel and Slow: Richmond captured after 3 days fighting, 30,000 men "left on the field.

author: alexander
old: Fourth of July 1862 — batteries firing, brigade harangued by Gen. Orders to move at moment's notice — leave tomorrow.

author: alexander
old: Fort Royal, VA — left Camp Goodrich July 5 at 5 PM, arrived 10 AM next day. Delayed by baggage trains.

author: henry
old: SEVEN DAYS RETREAT firsthand. was in a battle the last of June.
final: Writing from a camp on the James River after a late-June battle and the army's retreat — "if we call it such" — Henry recounts flinging away his knapsack on the double-quick and watching the regiment's Major lose both feet to a solid shot, faulting the want of judgment that placed them under the rebel batteries. Yet his sister's plans have raised his spirits, and he dreams of selling the farm to buy a team and ease their mother's life in Vermont. He burns every letter he receives now, and slips ten dollars into the envelope despite the risk.

author: henry
old: SEVEN DAYS RETREAT — extended detail. Sick ordered to hospital; McDonald came twice urging Henry to go; Henry stayed with the men.
final: Writing from camp near Harrison's Landing after the Seven Days' retreat, Henry recounts the double-quick into the woods, thrown knapsacks, and the bayonet charge where his regiment "fired very low and did great execution" — and the Irish Brigade storming a rebel battery, "a splendid sight, shouting at the top of their voices," though many men, supplies, and the battery itself were lost. Sick with worsening diarrhea, he twice refused McDonald's urging to go to the hospital, unwilling to leave the rest, while weighing the $100 bounty and land warrant binding him to finish his thirteen months.

author: alexander
old: Literary landscape description — Virginia from Pine Mountain summit: "green fields, meadows, large farms, patches of woods, roads winding here and there, little villages.

author: alexander
old: "FIRESIDE PATRIOTS" — Silas and Sid: "brave enough at home. " "The idea of men at home finding fault while we are doing the fighting!

author: james
old: JAMES AT WEST POINT — first extended description. Camp McRae on the plain.

author: henry
old: GRAND REVIEW of Army of the Potomac at Harrison's Landing — "last Tuesday" (July 22). Near James River, within sight of gunboats.
final: Henry describes the grand review of the Army of the Potomac near the James River the previous Tuesday — the regiments marched in line of battle within sight of the gunboats, the battery firing blank cartridges, an artist on hand whose sketch he expects in Harper's Weekly. Writing to his sister Frances, he confides a quieter wish: that peace might come "just before Sugar time" so he could farm again next spring, though he resigns himself to staying his time out — "there is no such luck for me." He signs off asking her to burn the scribble.

author: charles
old: CHARLES HUBBELL'S FIRST LETTER IN COLLECTION. Third brother to enter service.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF ANTIETAM — September 17, 1862. The bloodiest single day in American history.

author: james
old: CHARLES ENLISTED — James just learned, wants details. Hopes not as private; advises promotion-seeking.

author: mother
old: FIRST HOME-FRONT LETTER IN THE COLLECTION. Mother writes Henry four days after Antietam, reading casualty lists with trembling, thanking God his name hasn't appeared.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER HOSPITALIZED at Harpers Ferry. "Exhausting diarrhea for several weeks" combined with "severest military duty" — has "brought me pretty low.

author: mother
old: THE MOMENT MOTHER LEARNS. Between Sept 21 and Sept 28, Henry's name appeared on the published wounded list.

author: charles
old: Charles's first response to Henry's wounding. His theory — Henry is a prisoner at Richmond because the leg wound prevented escape — is a reasonable inference but unverified. He learned the news at 9 PM the previous night from "Alek Douglas." Expects to come home this week before mustering in.

author: charles
old: Most detailed description of training camp life in the collection. Charles describes Plattsburgh Barracks in architectural detail: stone buildings, two-story, 6 rooms long, bunks 4 high and 6 deep, straw ticks and blanke...

author: mcdonald
old: THE ONLY OUTSIDE VOICE IN THE COLLECTION. McDonald, Henry's tentmate in the 34th NY, writes Mother Hubbell to report what he knows of Henry after Antietam.

author: mother
old: MOTHER APPROACHES DESPAIR. She has received Alexander's Sept 19 letter (Henry missing after Antietam).

author: mother
old: NEW EYEWITNESS REPORT ON HENRY. Young Fiser says: "Henry was seen to fall, that the rebels were within two rods of them, they fled, and know nothing more of him.

author: charles
old: Charles returned from furlough to Plattsburgh. Received $25 check with $67 still owed. Double guards with loaded muskets to prevent desertion. Reports Alek Douglas's father severely hurt by falling timber. Still believes Henry is a prisoner. "Hoping that you & Frances will make the best of things."

author: luther
old: Routine correspondence between comrades. Luther recovering at Eckington Hospital, wants news of the company. Capt. Ransom visited with items from home — the same Ransom who took tea at the Hubbell home in Champlain (Oct 2–3) and is now returning to the regiment.

author: charles
old: CHARLES'S REGIMENT IDENTIFIED: 153rd New York Volunteers, Company I. Detailed journey from Plattsburgh to Camp Mohawk near Fonda, NY.

author: mother
old: THE PRISONER THEORY DIES. Misner, returned from Confederate captivity, tells Mother directly: he and Albert saw ALL the prisoners taken at Antietam, and Henry was NOT among them.

author: mother
old: FANNIE/FRANCES IDENTIFIED AS HUBBELL SISTER — signs "Aff. your sister, Fannie.

author: alexander
old: Alexander breaks a 46-day silence. After the hospital letter (Sept 27), his diarrhea evolved into jaundice, compounded by cold and a facial eruption threatening his eyesight. He has moved from hospital to Bolivar Heights to Harpers Ferry (guarding government property). He promises a longer letter when his eyes are stronger.

author: charles
old: Most detailed account of garrison duty in the collection. 153rd NY guards Alexandria, the convalescent camp, parole camp, and provides funeral escorts. Two regiments guarding the city; countersign required after 9 PM. Corporals reduced to ranks for AWOL and threatening an officer (tied to telegraph pole). Death of a soldier from Fonda — company raised $72 for embalming ($50) and freight ($25). Charles is managing family property from camp: timber, cedar, Plummer's debt. Frances teaching French. Also reveals "Jones" = James (wrote to him at West Point).

author: alexander
old: THE BROTHERS' REUNION. Alexander narrates finding Henry before Antietam — the only face-to-face meeting between the brothers described in the collection.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's most introspective letter. His description of feeling Mother's prayers during battle — "as tho I had a Mother upon her knees praying for me" while "shot and shell were shrieking and whirring around me" — is the collection's most vivid spiritual-combat passage. Thanksgiving on bean soup and hard tack while imagining Grandmother's dinner. Contempt for substitute-payers Whiteside and Doolittle. Government hasn't paid them; needs money again.

author: charles
old: Charles's first letter to Frances directly. Soldiers' cemetery description — "buried as close as possible in straight rows," headboards of "durable wood furnished by Government." Frenchman died, company couldn't raise money to send body home, buried in soldiers' cemetery. Lice prevention with unguentum. Thanksgiving on guard duty at a bridge. Mentions encouraging news about Henry from McDonald (details unclear) but doubts it: "too good to be true."

author: charles
old: Bounty system detailed — Charles breaks down his $67: $60 state, $28 county, $10 town, $2 enlistment fee. Fonda men received $200 town bounty plus $4/month. Self-inflicted wounds to avoid duty — two men shot fingers off "accidentally," another shot thumb and two fingers, another shot through arm. Exchanging Austrian rifle muskets for new guns. Band formed with soldier-bought instruments. Gen. Slough as military governor of Alexandria; Capt. Rich on his staff. McDonald to write his wife about Henry information.

author: charles
old: McDONALD'S STORY CONFIRMED FALSE. Charles traces the information chain: McDonald → someone → Champlain → army friends → back to source.

author: mother
old: McDONALD'S REPORT DEBUNKED. Mother now says "it turns out that McDonald has heard false rumor.

author: mcdonald
old: McDONALD REVEALS HIS SOURCE — AND IT'S A CHAIN OF HEARSAY. His information about Henry being alive came from Charles (of the 60th — i.

author: alexander
old: THE BEST EYEWITNESS ACCOUNT OF HENRY'S WOUNDING. Alexander visited the 34th NY camp and reports: "the boys said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and threw himself down.

author: charles
old: ALEXANDER VISITS CHARLES — CHRISTMAS 1862. Alexander arrived by railroad from Fairfax Station (15 miles) on Christmas Day at 4 PM, left next morning at 11 AM.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER AT FAIRFAX STATION. Detailed description of Alexander's camp conditions: water from ditches, 60th NY called "the thieving reg't," $11 sutler debt, six months unpaid.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's destitution put in perspective — he has been worse. "I have seen the time when I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night." March orders received evening of Jan 13 — 12 hours notice, "probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans." The religious commendation is notable: "We are all in God's hands."

author: james
old: OFFICER'S PERSPECTIVE ON THE HUBBELL FAMILY. Captain Ransom writes directly to Mother to reassure her about Alexander — "never looked so finely and well.

author: charles
old: PAY RECEIVED — FIRST IN MONTHS. Two months' pay received; three more owed.

author: alexander
old: CAMP MOVED TO STAFFORD HOUSE. The 60th NY has marched from Fairfax Station to near Stafford House — closer to Fredericksburg.

author: charles
old: HOOKER'S ARMY REORGANIZATION. Pennsylvania reserves reduced from 15,000 to 2,300 — passing through Alexandria.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER GOT HIS FURLOUGH. The application denied by Sigel in early February was apparently approved by the War Department.

author: charles
old: OFFICER CONFLICT IN 153rd NY. Armstrong resigned after difficulty with the Colonel, who is under arrest.

author: alexander
old: POST-FURLOUGH REFLECTIONS. Alexander reliving his home visit in imagination.

author: charles
old: 12-15 women living with husbands in the 153rd NY — drawing rations, washing clothes for pay. "A stout woman was marching through the mud after her husband.

author: alexander
old: COMPLETE OFFICER TURNOVER IN CO. Ransom gone (Feb 6), both Lieutenants resigned — new Captain is Lieut.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER AT AQUIA CREEK. Brothers meet again — Alexander "hearty as a buck," big fat face, pleased about furlough.

author: alexander
old: MAIL MISDIRECTION. Mother's letter with money for Charles (153rd NY) was misrouted to Alexander (60th NY) — postmaster confusion between regiments.

author: charles
old: HENRY DEATH ACCEPTANCE ADVANCING. "I am afraid he was killed" — Charles's most direct statement yet.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S OPTIMISM PEAKS. Expects "honorable discharge...

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER REFUSES MOTHER'S PLEA FOR SAFETY. Mother asked Alexander to write the surgeon for "a place of safety in time of battle" — Alexander's response is fierce: "Would you have me branded as a coward?

author: charles
old: "I AM AFRAID THAT HE WAS KILLED. " Charles's second direct statement about Henry's death.

author: charles
old: THIRD "I AM AFRAID HE WAS KILLED" STATEMENT. Charles now adds counterfactual: "If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in.

author: mcneil
old: MICHIGAN PERSPECTIVE ON THE WAR. Cousin Mary from Atlas, MI: draft resistance, anti-emancipation sentiment ("sooner fight for the Union than to free the negroes"), high civilian mortality, truce hopes.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER STILL HOPES HENRY IS ALIVE. While Charles has said three times "I am afraid he was killed," Alexander clings to hope: "It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field.

author: alexander
old: MAJOR MONEY TRANSFER. $40 by express + $7.

author: alexander
old: HENRY'S CHARACTER FROM 34th NY COMRADE. A soldier from Henry's old regiment (34th NY) describes Henry's moral code: refused to take plundered goods — "the partaker is as bad as the thief.

author: charles
old: HENRY'S GRAVE MARKER REPORTED. Abram Fry (NY artillery) claims to have seen Henry's name on a headboard at his grave on the Antietam battlefield.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S FORMAL INQUIRY — THE ONLY LETTER FROM HER PEN IN THE COLLECTION. Hubbell writes to an unknown authority (possibly Sanitary Commission, military records, or hospital official) to trace Henry.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S GRIEF — THE MOST EMOTIONALLY RAW DOCUMENT IN THE COLLECTION. Mother reads Henry's letters for the first time since his death — "I have wept until I am almost blind.

author: charles
old: CHANCELLORSVILLE CASUALTIES — 60th NY. 73 total: 9 killed, 43 wounded, 21 missing.

author: charles
old: CHARLES SEARCHES FOR ALEXANDER AFTER CHANCELLORSVILLE. Went to Aquia Creek but couldn't find Alex — heard 60th was about a mile from landing.

author: alexander
old: DETAILED CHANCELLORSVILLE CASUALTY LIST FOR CO. Brookway wounded; I.

author: charles
old: POST-CHANCELLORSVILLE REORGANIZATION. Burdick promoted to Captain; officer chain reorganized — Major to Col.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER — DETAILED CHANCELLORSVILLE AFTERMATH. Alexander was color bearer in the fight.

author: alexander
old: REDINGTON PORTRAIT — SINGING DURING SHELLFIRE. Alexander describes Col.

author: charles
old: "APPLY AT ONCE FOR HENRY'S BACK PAY AND BOUNTY. HE WAS KILLED, WITHOUT A DOUBT.

author: charles
old: Fragment only. Mother has left home to visit Charlotte. Frances is alone. June 29, 1863 — two days before the Battle of Gettysburg begins. Alexander's regiment is on the march.

author: alexander
old: GETTYSBURG — FIRST-PERSON BATTLE REPORT. Alexander survived the Battle of Gettysburg without a scratch.

author: charles
old: July 4th grand parade in Alexandria — troops marched with whiskey rations. Charles hasn't heard from Alexander and doesn't yet know about Gettysburg. Henry's bounty application urged. Deserter caught through wife's letter — nabbed in St. Lawrence County.

author: alexander
old: POST-GETTYSBURG — TWO STANDS OF COLORS CAPTURED. The 60th NY captured two Confederate battle flags — a significant combat achievement.

author: charles
old: NEW YORK CITY DRAFT RIOTS referenced — "Don't you think New York has been a pleasant place to live in the last few days? " (July 13-16, 1863).

author: charles
old: Moved from Alexandria to Capitol Hill Barracks — detached from regiment for six months. Ration theft scandal — orderly sergeant, corporal James Lucas, and cook arrested. Col. very strict. Charles first learns Alexander survived Gettysburg through Mother's letter, not Alexander's.

author: alexander
old: GETTYSBURG COMBAT DETAIL — P. provides vivid firsthand account: "fifty or sixty shots into the very teeth of the rebels.

author: alexander
old: Draft enforcement in Washington — citizens caught fleeing at R.R. Depot, young man arrested dressed as captain. Reg't guards two prisons and depot. James Lucas punished for ration theft (reduced to ranks, lost month's pay). Burdick resigned. Whiskey rations with quinine — antimalarial.

author: charles
old: Garrison life in Washington barracks — bed bugs, guard duty, draft enforcement. Charlotte visit suggested for Mother. Financial details — Savage debts, Surrogate office money, cow sale to Boyle. War assessment: "Jeff is about played out" but guerrilla fighting remains.

author: alexander
old: ANTIETAM BATTLEFIELD — ALEXANDER PASSED OVER IT. how I longed to leave the ranks and hunt for some trace of Henry, but it was impossible.

author: alexander
old: "COULD YOU SUPPOSE I COULD EVER FORGET MY OLD HOME AND MY MOTHER? " Alexander's most emotionally raw letter to Mother.

author: charles
old: Garrison life — church services, library, bed bugs. James at West Point — 65 new cadets to fill southern vacancies. Burdick gone home. Methodist church incident — soldier drunk in church.

author: charles
old: James's West Point demerits explained. Corporal died — sickness in regiment. Pet Steais hospitalized. Anecdote about soldier swindled by fiancée — $200 lost. Free library access.

author: alexander
old: EXECUTION OF DESERTERS — EYEWITNESS. Two men shot; one required three volleys.

author: charles
old: Garrison details. Pension advice — "with three sons in the army it looks bad." Alex Douglas likely to be discharged. Wife arrived at barracks — "What in hell did you come for!" James's demerits corrected. Mrs. Brikerhoff companion for Mother. Frances "teaches too constantly."

author: charles
old: ALEXANDER HEADING TO TENNESSEE — 11th and 12th Corps reinforcing Rosecrans (after Chickamauga). Alexander said "he did not care where they went, while they were riding they were not fighting.

author: alexander
old: FIRST LETTER FROM TENNESSEE. Alexander at Murfreesboro as garrison.

author: charles
old: COLORED ODD FELLOWS PARADE in Washington — Black fraternal organization marching with uniforms, banners, band. Police present to protect them.

author: charles
old: BELLE BOYD — famous Confederate spy confined at Carroll Prison. Charles on guard duty when woman in broadcloth pants visited Boyd.

author: charles
old: Furlough offered but declined — no money ($1.50). Election furloughs — soldiers going home to vote in NY elections. Cough/illness for a week. Money lost — $5 from vest pocket. Socks sufficient. Reg't singing "Let me kiss him for his mother." Steais in hospital again — breast complaint.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF WAUHATCHIE (October 28-29, 1863) — Alexander's brigade attacked at night by Confederate forces. Greene seriously wounded — the hero of Culp's Hill at Gettysburg.

author: mother
old: SECOND MOTHER'S LETTER IN COLLECTION. Joy at receiving Alexander's Nov.

author: charles
old: 1,846 REBEL PRISONERS transported to Old Capitol prison — reg't up all night. Some taken to Point Lookout.

author: charles
old: $18.78 stolen from pocket book — someone found it with money, returned it empty. $20 check enclosed for Mother. Clothing account settled — $2.70 surplus from $42/year allowance. Col. trying for Philadelphia; may go to Alexandria or Chattanooga. New guns replacing old ones.

author: alexander
old: DISCHARGE EFFORT — CAPT. RANSOM INTERCEDING.

author: alexander
old: WOUNDED AT LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN — "BATTLE ABOVE THE CLOUDS" (November 24, 1863). Alexander hit by minie ball in left side — "rather a close call for my life.

author: charles
old: Charles aware of Chattanooga fighting — "Hooker's fight" — but doesn't know Alexander was wounded. Half rations. Pocket book saga continues — check system explained in detail. Thanksgiving dinner: mashed potatoes and milk gravy. Milk women selling at 10¢/qt.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S AGONY — DOES NOT KNOW IF ALEXANDER IS ALIVE. Oh, where are you?

author: charles
old: Garrison routine — Carroll Prison guard duty resumed. Union church formed — all denominations, mostly Methodist. Congress in session — Charles plans to attend. Gen. Slough's "band box regt." Theater passes. Still no news from Alexander after Lookout Mountain.

author: alexander
old: COMPREHENSIVE BATTLE NARRATIVE — WAUHATCHIE, LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN, MISSIONARY RIDGE, RINGGOLD. Alexander recounts the 60th NY's engagements since arriving in Tennessee.

author: alexander
old: Alexander back with regiment — left hospital early. Side still sore. Half rations — supply problems. Confirms Co. H losses at Missionary Ridge and Ringgold: Doten and Housedean killed, Lemage and Small wounded (Small lost leg). Sergt. Long confirmed unhurt. Expects to move soon.

author: charles
old: New Year's and Christmas celebrations — turkey dinner, lager beer, flour pudding. Re-enlistment bounties — $1,000 for three years; Charles advises Alex not to re-enlist. Marching orders to Harper's Ferry countermanded. Turkey theft. Geo. Dodds visited from hospital.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER RE-ENLISTED AND LEFT DETACHMENT "CLANDESTINELY. " Technically reported as a deserter — but deserted his detachment to rejoin his regiment.

author: charles
old: REGIMENTAL SCANDAL. Davis and Adjutant under arrest — court martial for bucking and gagging, trying to remove U.

author: charles
old: Guard bribed $200 to let prisoner escape — sentry in prison, rumor he will be shot. Charles attended Congressional debate on confiscation — Democrat vs. Republican. Love feast in church — soldiers attending for girls. $450 town bounty discussion. Sidney's family trouble.

author: charles
old: POINT LOOKOUT PRISONER CAMP. Charles escorted ~400 rebel prisoners to Point Lookout — camp holds ~8,000.

author: charles
old: LEAVING WASHINGTON FOR ALEXANDRIA. Sudden orders — regiment relieved from guard duty.

author: alexander
old: Transit through Nashville — visited Thos. Small at hospital, lost leg at Ringgold. Luther's bounty spending. Comfortable passenger cars instead of freight cars.

author: alexander
old: REBEL CAPTAIN CONVERSATION — Confederate conscription: "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts.

author: alexander
old: Confederate hasty evacuation — guns left unmuzzled, carriages burned, enormous rifled guns on track. Kilpatrick's raid disrupted railroads. Sherman on the move. 60-mile march to reach this location. Immense ordnance abandoned.

author: charles
old: 153rd NY ARRIVES IN LOUISIANA. Sea voyage from Alexandria via steamship Mississippi — entered Mississippi River mouth on 4th day.

author: charles
old: CHARLES DETACHED AS CLERK AT GEN. Mother's letter-writing campaign succeeded — Mrs.

author: alexander
old: REBEL DESERTERS' TESTIMONY. Johnson's army suffering for food — one day's ration scarcely enough for one meal.

author: alexander
old: Personal letter to sister. Playful tone. Yearning for civilian life — "the proudest day of my life."

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S MOST LITERARY LETTER. Vivid panoramic description of camp — picket fires, earthworks, brass battery gleaming, Brigade band, drums, Guard Mounting, dinner call, dress parade, Tattoo, Taps.

author: charles
old: RED RIVER CAMPAIGN — victories at Fort DeRussy and Alexandria reported. Fox dismissed for disloyalty and conduct unbecoming.

author: alexander
old: Warrant renewed — old position in 60th Veterans. Marching orders for Chattanooga or Knoxville. Requests boots and stamps.

author: charles
old: Charles's comfortable clerk life at Banks HQ — sleeping on office floor with marble mantle and washstand. Extra pay $11 for first month. Banks and staff in the field (Red River). Roses blooming in March. Red River Campaign — "expect to clear rebels out."

author: alexander
old: 20TH ARMY CORPS FORMED — 11th and 12th Corps consolidated under Hooker. Slocum to Vicksburg.

author: alexander
old: BASEBALL IN THE CIVIL WAR — "UNION BASE. " Two regiments challenged the 60th NY to a game of "Union Base" — a kind of game of ball.

author: charles
old: RED RIVER CAMPAIGN BATTLE REPORT — "terrible fighting in western Louisiana" — victory "so bloody we were not able to take advantage of it. " 153rd NY was in it.

author: alexander
old: JAMES HAS ENLISTED. Alexander assesses James's chances — doubts cavalry, thinks he'll rise to straps (officer).

author: alexander
old: 20TH ARMY CORPS ORDER OF BATTLE. Complete brigade composition listed.

author: charles
old: CHARLES RELIEVED FROM HQ — RETURNING TO REGIMENT. Penmanship not good enough.

author: charles
old: BROTHER-TO-BROTHER LETTER — rare front-to-front correspondence. Expanded clerk death account — burial scene with wagon of 8 bodies, clerk's prayer, volleys, streetcar home.

author: alexander
old: EVE OF ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — ALEXANDER'S FAREWELL. "It is the death struggle of this mighty rebellion.

author: charles
old: GUERRILLA WARFARE ON RED RIVER. Steamer fired upon — 1 killed, 1 wounded on boat.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — FIRST LETTER FROM GEORGIA. "Close upon the enemy.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — ALTOONA CREEK. Alexander in Georgia, still safe.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF BUZZARD'S ROOST / ROCKY FACE RIDGE. Detailed tactical account — 1st & 2nd Brigades engaged, 3rd Brigade on cavalry support reconnaissance.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF RESACA (May 13-15, 1864). Alexander came through unscathed.

author: alexander
old: BASS SHOT — probably fatally. The schoolteacher/Southern sympathizer from Champlain has been shot (by Dodds?

author: charles
old: JAMES HUBBELL ARRIVES — JOINS CHARLES'S REGIMENT. Three brothers now confirmed in active service.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF DALLAS / NEW HOPE CHURCH (May 25-June 4). Writing under fire — "there goes one now — b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l.

author: charles
old: JAMES HUBBELL — LANCE CORPORAL. Already promoted, drilling recruits.

author: alexander
old: SIX LETTERS FROM HOME after weeks without mail. Bass recovering — shooting described humorously.

author: charles
old: Foraging expedition — 15 miles, two regiments, wagon train. Corn taken from barns — women objected. Money sent home: Charles $50, James $330, Joseph Martin $20 for wife. James's bounty details. Pay increase rumor — $16/month from May 1.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — NEAR MARIETTA, APPROACHING KENNESAW MOUNTAIN. Fighting nearly every day.

author: james
old: JAMES HUBBELL'S FIRST LETTER. The youngest brother writes for the first time in the collection.

author: charles
old: Brief note appended to James's letter. Dr. Sweeney — saw Frances recently. Express charges: $4 freight + $2 insurance on $400.

author: charles
old: Camp economics — butter, flour, dried apples, pies, doughnuts. James making doughnuts (heavy — no yeast powder). New York papers 25¢. Chaplain says won't stay long — garrison somewhere near Mississippi.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — NEAR MARIETTA. Sherman's flanking tactics — "comes around on the blind side.

author: alexander
old: LUTHER WOUNDED — ball tore furrow in right side, passed through right arm above elbow. Not dangerous — two or three months recovery.

author: alexander
old: SAW ATLANTA FROM A RIDGE — spires, chimneys, smoke from furnaces, forts, rifle pits visible. Near Chattahoochee River.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF PEACHTREE CREEK (July 20, 1864). Rebs defeated with great loss — dead and wounded left on field.

author: alexander
old: "ATLANTA EXPRESS" — battery fires shell into Atlanta every five minutes through the night. Sherman ordered batteries silent during the day, then opened at 10 P.

author: alexander
old: 23RD CORPS MOVING TO RIGHT — Schofield's movement toward Macon & Atlanta railroad. Lines within half mile of the railroad.

author: alexander
old: HOOKER LEAVES 20TH CORPS — farewell ride along the line. Pennsylvania soldier with leg shot off calls out "Good bye, General Hooker!

author: alexander
old: MOST DETAILED PEACHTREE CREEK ACCOUNT — rebels in solid columns, "seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. " Changed front three times.

author: james
old: EARLY'S RAID ON WASHINGTON — 153rd NY sent from Louisiana to Washington defenses. Placed in rifle pits.

author: alexander
old: SCURVY — Alexander hospitalized near Atlanta. Surgeon says very young for it.

author: charles
old: SHERIDAN'S ARMY FORMS — 19th, 6th, and 8th Corps under Sheridan with large cavalry force near Harper's Ferry. Haven't engaged rebs yet — cavalry has fought some.

author: alexander
old: FALL OF ATLANTA IMMINENT — 20th Corps fallen back to Chattahoochee line. Rest of army on "grand flanking excursion" toward Macon.

author: alexander
old: WHEELER'S RAID — Confederate cavalry tore up railroad, preventing hospital train from reaching Nashville. Stopped at Chattanooga.

author: alexander
old: 60TH NY VETS ESCORT PAYMASTER — regiment comes through Chattanooga. Government owes Alexander $240.

author: charles
old: THIRD BATTLE OF WINCHESTER (Sept 19, 1864) — "battle near Winchester two days since. 4 killed, 12 wounded in company.

author: alexander
old: THREE-YEAR ANNIVERSARY — September 21, 1861 to September 21, 1864. "Three long — long — weary years!

author: alexander
old: Brief note to Frances — apology for not writing. Not feeling well.

author: alexander
old: MOST EXTENSIVE RACIAL/POLITICAL COMMENTARY in collection. Border state soldiers' views on "nigger equality" — would free slaves but send them out of country.

author: james
old: SHENANDOAH CAMPAIGN — Third Winchester and Fisher's Hill described from James's perspective. Pursuit — burning rebel wagons, demoralized enemy.

author: charles
old: $1,202 BOUNTY for one-year recruit — inflation of bounties by late 1864. SHERIDAN'S BURNING — cavalry burned barns and grist mills to Staunton.

author: alexander
old: STRAW POLL ON HOSPITAL TRAIN — 37 Lincoln, 5 McClellan. Lincoln "the favored one.

author: charles
old: BATTLE OF CEDAR CREEK (October 19, 1864) — one of the war's most dramatic battles. SURPRISE ATTACK — rebs got behind breastworks before they knew it.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER FOR LINCOLN — "square and fair for Abraham Lincoln. " The McClellan devotee of April 1864 has completed his political shift.

author: james
old: JAMES'S CEDAR CREEK ACCOUNT — wounded in left thigh, walked miles to avoid capture. Complete rout of 8th Corps, surprise attack, then Union rally — "three times terribly whipped" in the Valley.

author: charles
old: GRANDMOTHER'S DEATH. Post-Cedar Creek camp life — drill, dress parade.

author: charles
old: SEVEN MONTHS PAY — $108 received Dec 9. Winter quarters at Newtown — stone fireplace, chimney.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF NASHVILLE IMMINENT — Hood in front of the city. Building breastworks.

author: james
old: CHESTNUT HILL HOSPITAL — Philadelphia. Wound nearly healed.

author: charles
old: Practical boot transaction — bought government cavalry boots for $5. Six inches of snow. Expects to move to guard railroad. Mittens with one finger requested.

author: alexander
old: THREE DAYS BEFORE BATTLE OF NASHVILLE. Beyond pickets for firewood — "was not fired at.

author: charles
old: FALL OF SAVANNAH — brigade gave rousing cheers. Alexander lucky to miss 500-mile march.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S JOY AT ALEXANDER'S SURVIVAL — feared dead at Nashville. CHAMPLAIN UNDER MILITARY RULE — 150 soldiers, cavalry stables, pickets, borders sealed against Canada (post-St.

author: charles
old: POST-WAR OCCUPATION — 153rd NY sent from Washington to Savannah for occupation duty. River obstructed with piles and forts.

author: alexander
old: POST-WAR DEMOBILIZATION. Corps and division broken up.

author: alexander
old: 60TH NY VETS MUSTERED OUT. "The long wished for order came.

author: charles
old: POST-WAR SAVANNAH — July 4th, 1865: all-black fire company parade, "the darkeys young and old all turned out. " Cotton being hauled 160 miles to Savannah.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S LAST LETTER — THE HOMECOMING. Camp Wheeler, Ogdensburgh — the same place he enlisted in September 1861.

author: mother
old: POST-WAR LIFE — 1870. Five years after the war.
